routes.label: Compute the pentagon's area in two ways

question:
\(ABCDE\) is a regular pentagon. \(AP,\) \(AQ\) and \(AR\) are the perpendiculars dropped from \(A\) onto \(CD,\) \(CB\) extended and \(DE\) extended, respectively. Let \(O\) be the center of the pentagon. If \(OP=1,\) then \(AO+AQ+AR\) equals

[Figure 1](figures/1986_AMC_12_Q28_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The three perpendiculars are heights of triangles whose bases are sides of the pentagon. Since those sides have equal lengths, comparing areas will produce a sum of the heights without finding them individually.

[Figure 1](figures/1986_AMC_12_Q28_question_fig1.svg)

Let the common side length be \(s>0\), and let the pentagon's area be \(K\). In a regular pentagon, the symmetry axis through \(A\) and the center \(O\) meets the opposite side \(CD\) perpendicularly at its midpoint. Thus this intersection is \(P\), and \(OP=1\) is the perpendicular distance from the center to each side.

Joining \(O\) to all five vertices partitions the pentagon into five triangles, each with base \(s\) and height \(1\). Hence
\[
K=5\left(\frac12s\cdot1\right)=\frac52s.
\]
Alternatively, diagonals \(AC\) and \(AD\) partition the convex pentagon into triangles \(ABC\), \(ACD\), and \(ADE\). Their bases \(BC\), \(CD\), and \(DE\) all have length \(s\). Their corresponding heights are \(AQ\), \(AP\), and \(AR\); a perpendicular to an extended base still gives the triangle's height. These triangles fill the pentagon without overlapping interiors, so
\[
K=\frac12s(AQ+AP+AR).
\]
Equating the two expressions and dividing by \(s/2>0\) gives
\[
AQ+AP+AR=5.
\]
The points \(A,O,P\) are collinear with \(O\) between \(A\) and \(P\), so \(AP=AO+OP=AO+1\). Therefore
\[
AO+AQ+AR=5-1=\boxed{4},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{C}\).
